strengths: Significance: The paper usefully decouples the forward diffusion horizon from the desired sampling accuracy. The initial Langevin correction permits a fixed T1, and Theorem 5.1 removes a logarithmic accuracy dependence from the sampling-step bound relative to the cited baseline.

Originality: The strongest contribution is the score-confinement and truncation argument in Theorem 4.2. It converts endpoint L2 score accuracy into control of an exponential-moment loss, providing useful understanding beyond the predictor-corrector algorithm itself.

Soundness: The central argument combines quantitative log-Sobolev regularization, inexact Langevin convergence, and reverse-process error propagation coherently. Appendices B–D provide substantial supporting derivations, and the Wasserstein analysis accommodates norm-subgaussian targets without requiring the original distribution to satisfy a functional inequality.

Presentation: The algorithm, error decomposition, and roles of T1, T2, and early stopping are explained clearly. The manuscript explicitly distinguishes its continuous-time Wasserstein result from its discretized stochastic result. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b08/review-experiment-a2yoyroa/call-aa0fb93dd6784b9896d6097d107e83ef/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Reproducibility and ethics: Explicit assumptions, step sizes, and extensive proofs support reproduction of the theoretical analysis. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the mathematical work and synthetic examples.
weaknesses: Soundness and claim scope: Wasserstein convergence is not established from L2 accuracy alone. Theorem 4.1 retains I_tau(t) = exp(t - tau + integral L_s), and the discussion on page 8 adds a boundedness assumption along improving estimator sequences. L2 convergence does not imply this regularity condition. Its behavior as early stopping vanishes remains unquantified, limiting the advertised general convergence guarantee.

Significance of the complexity comparison: Theorem 4.2 requires separate endpoint accuracy b(T1), which the integrated training loss alone does not control. Using its sufficient condition to make the exponential-moment error O(eta²) imposes b(T1) of order eta^(4+72βδ²). Thus the sampling-step improvement comes with a substantially stricter endpoint accuracy prescription; reduced training cost or total computational cost is not established.

Presentation and scope: The abstract and conclusion overstate the logarithmic dimension dependence. That dependence describes the required horizon T1; the full bounds retain explicit dimension factors and potentially large Lipschitz-dependent amplification. Moreover, Theorem 5.1 requires uniformly Lipschitz true scores and treats a stochastic reverse process, leaving discretization of the principal Wasserstein/ODE result unresolved.

Empirical reproducibility: Figure 1 omits the numerical T1 values, score-model and training details, integration settings, sample counts, Wasserstein estimation procedure, and meaning of its error bars. It also lacks comparisons at matched computational budgets. Decreasing Wasserstein errors do not establish the accompanying claim that the untruncated estimator has small exponential-moment error, since that quantity is not measured.

Technical presentation: Several formulas require correction. Lemma D.1 omits the exponential inside the logarithmic expectation, making its literal statement invalid even for an exact score. Lemma 4.4 and its proof use M² despite defining M as the second moment. These appear repairable, but should be corrected for reliable reuse.
